hints: Focus on what you are told after one division in 14N: 100% of the DNA is hybrid with one 15N strand and one 14N strand. What will happen when each of those strands is used as a template again?
Remember DNA replication is semi-conservative, so each old strand is kept and a new strand is made using only 14N from the new medium.
walkthrough:
**Recall the starting point**

This is the famous Meselson and Stahl experiment. You start with all heavy DNA, so both strands are $^{15}N$.

Think of it as: $^{15}N$ / $^{15}N$.

**Understand the first division**

After one division in $^{14}N$, each new DNA keeps one old $^{15}N$ strand and gains one new $^{14}N$ strand. That is why you get 100% hybrid DNA.

Hybrid = $^{15}N$ / $^{14}N$.

**Follow the second division**

Now each hybrid DNA unwinds again in $^{14}N$ medium. The $^{15}N$ strand makes another hybrid, but the $^{14}N$ strand makes a fully light DNA.

So from 2 hybrid molecules you get: 2 hybrid + 2 light ($^{14}N$ / $^{14}N$). That is 2 out of 4, or 50% hybrid DNA.

options.A: Too low. 25% hybrid would be the result after three divisions in 14N, not two.
options.B: Correct. After the second division, half the DNA is hybrid (15N/14N) and half is light (14N/14N), so 50% hybrid.
options.C: Too high. The proportion of hybrid DNA halves with each division after the first, it does not stay at 75%.
options.D: This was true after the first division, but after the second division some fully light 14N DNA is also made.
